citation: Tajiri K, Takahashi K, Ikeda K, Tomita K. Common Peroneal Nerve Block for Sciatica. Clin Orthop Relat Res 1998;347:203-207
text_quality: ocr — the PDF is a scan with no text layer and no OCR engine is installed in this session, so texts/S-686-33.txt is a manual transcription from the five page images in texts/scans/. Abstract, methods, results, both tables, all figure legends, the discussion and all 16 references are transcribed; Figures 1 and 2 are per-subject line plots whose individual values exist only as plotted points, and Table 2 carries the group means, so nothing numeric is lost.
design: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled parallel-group trial. Patients randomised to lidocaine or saline after enrolment; the physician assessing the effect of the block had no knowledge of the type of therapy given. Student's t test for pain scores, Spearman correlation for the pin-prick/pain relationship, significance at p < 0.01.
population: 22 consecutive outpatients with sciatic radicular pain on physical examination and intervertebral disc herniation at L4-L5 or L5-S1 confirmed on myelography or MRI, enrolled October 1991 to March 1992. Three lidocaine-group patients were excluded for showing no change of muscle strength and sensation at 15 minutes, leaving 19 analysed.
n: lidocaine n = 9 (mean age 41.8, range 22-69); placebo n = 10 (mean age 41.0, range 18-70); 22 enrolled, 3 excluded
setting: Outpatients; study performed at the School of Medicine, Kanazawa University, Japan
intervention: Common peroneal nerve block near the fibular head, injected distal to the fibular head: lidocaine [dose figure omitted] in one arm, physiologic saline [dose figure omitted] in the other. Injection was placed near the nerve at a site that did not cause radiating pain.
comparator: Physiologic saline, same volume and site (placebo injection)
route: Perineural injection at the common peroneal nerve near the fibular head. This is a peripheral nerve block, not an intradermal wheal.
duration: Single block. Pain and the straight leg raising test were measured before the block and at 15 minutes after it. There is no later follow-up and no measurement after the block wore off.
outcomes: Five-grade pain scale for lower leg pain (0 none to 4 unbearable); straight leg raising test in degrees; pin-prick sensitivity and manual muscle testing of tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus as indicators of blockade

key_results.quote: The intensity of pain in the lower leg was determined before and at 15 minutes after nerve block using a five grade pain scale
Patients who showed no changes of sensation and muscle strength at 15 minutes after nerve block were excluded from this study.
The average pain scale score decreased from 3.1 to 0.6, indicating that leg pain decreased significantly after the block (p < 0.001).
The average pain scale score changed slightly from 3.0 to 2.6, and leg pain did not decrease significantly after the block.
There was a significant difference between the two groups in the reduction of lower leg pain (p < 0.001).
The physician assessing the effect of the block had no knowledge of the type of therapy given.
The decrease in sensitivity to pin prick test did not show any significant relationship to the decrease of pain.

author_limitations.quote: A placebo effect has been reported to occur in one of three cases.3 In this study, lower leg pain decreased in four of 10 patients in the placebo group.
The mechanism of the generation of sciatic radicular pain remains unknown.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Xavier AV, McDanal J, Kissin I. Relief of sciatic radicular pain by sciatic nerve block. Anesth Analg 1988;67(12):1177-1180
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: the closest precedent for a local-anaesthetic nerve block relieving radicular pain, and the obvious candidate for the relief-outlasting-the-block question behind D020. Verified in Europe PMC: PMID 3269220, DOI 10.1213/00000539-198812000-00013, publication types Journal Article and Case Reports, no abstract indexed, 15 citing papers, two published comments (PMIDs 2764297 and 2818739). Being a case series it is uncontrolled, so it cannot displace a sham-controlled demonstration.
